- **Keep working through a multi-step plan without pausing for approval of each step** — aggregate the steps into one substantial change to review, and stop only for an action that reaches the world (a release, a fleet-wide effect, anything irreversible) or a decision only the owner can make.

## github
The GitHub MCP Server provides tools to interact with GitHub platform.

Tool selection guidance:
	1. Use 'list_*' tools for broad, simple retrieval and pagination of all items of a type (e.g., all issues, all PRs, all branches) with basic filtering.
	2. Use 'search_*' tools for targeted queries with specific criteria, keywords, or complex filters (e.g., issues with certain text, PRs by author, code containing functions).

Context management:
	1. Use pagination whenever possible with batches of 5-10 items.
	2. Use minimal_output parameter set to true if the full information is not needed to accomplish a task.

Tool usage guidance:
	1. For 'search_*' tools: Use separate 'sort' and 'order' parameters if available for sorting results - do not include 'sort:' syntax in query strings. Query strings should contain only search criteria (e.g., 'org:google language:python'), not sorting instructions. Always call 'get_me' first to understand current user permissions and context. ## Issues

Check 'list_issue_types' first for organizations to use proper issue types. Use 'search_issues' before creating new issues to avoid duplicates. Always set 'state_reason' when closing issues. ## Pull Requests

PR review workflow: Always use 'pull_request_review_write' with method 'create' to create a pending review, then 'add_comment_to_pending_review' to add comments, and finally 'pull_request_review_write' with method 'submit_pending' to submit the review for complex reviews with line-specific comments.

Before creating a pull request, search for pull request templates in the repository. Template files are called pull_request_template.md or they're located in '.github/PULL_REQUEST_TEMPLATE' directory. Use the template content to structure the PR description and then call create_pull_request tool.

# Growth — discover local packs (per repo)

A weekly reflection on **this repo's own** captured knowledge: knowing the Claudinite packs already available to it, notice when project-specific knowledge is worth organizing into a **new local pack** — and author it. A local operation: it writes only the repo's **own** `.claudinite/local/packs/`, landing through a PR **a human reviews** (unlike [growth-extract](../growth-extract/task.md), which lands unreviewed where the repo's delivery settings allow; the shared canon stays human-gated too — lifting a local pack up is the central promote task's job). Finding nothing new worth a pack is a perfectly good, common outcome.

There is no windowed Context to bind — the opportunity is standing (knowledge that was never organized into a pack, not a recent change), so examine the repo as it is.

This run opens a PR and **never arms auto-merge**. Extract may land unreviewed because it adds prose or a rule to territory a local pack already owns; a **new pack** ships new `.mjs` conformance checks that run at every Stop and in CI the moment it merges — a check can break CI, so it's reviewed, exactly as the sibling [prose-to-checks-sweep](../prose-to-checks-sweep/task.md) is.

# Reusable workflow: builds a repo's privacy policy into a one-page GitHub
# Pages site and deploys it at the fixed permalink /privacy/ —
#   https://<owner>.github.io/<repo>/privacy/
# The Jekyll `permalink` pins that public path independent of where PRIVACY.md
# lives in the repo (move the file → only the input below changes, never the
# URL). The page body is the caller's PRIVACY.md verbatim — the single source
# of truth, no duplicated copy.
#
# Deliberately NOT Chrome-specific (hence the unprefixed name): any publish
# standard whose store listing needs a live privacy-policy URL deploys through
# it. Vendored into the extension repo by the chrome-extension-release pack;
# workflow_call ONLY. It is invoked by "Chrome extension: Publish to Chrome Web
# Store" (uses: ./.github/workflows/deploy-privacy-page.yml) so the page is
# refreshed whenever the listing ships (and, because that publish workflow runs
# this leg even when the upload leg fails, it's also how the /privacy/ URL first
# goes live before the first publication). There is no standalone privacy
# dispatch stub — a repo never calls this directly.
#
# One-time owner setup in the calling repo: Pages source = "GitHub Actions"
# (repo Settings → Pages). Production deploys only from the default branch (the
# github-pages environment's branch policy), so the calling stub must be on
# `main` to publish.
#
# The calling job must grant `permissions: contents: read, pages: write,
# id-token: write, issues: write` (Pages deploy + the failure reporter).
name: Deploy privacy policy to GitHub Pages (reusable)

on:
  workflow_call:
    inputs:
      privacy_md_path:
        description: "Repo-relative path of the privacy policy Markdown"
        required: false
        type: string
        default: dev/build/release/store_artifacts/PRIVACY.md

# Least privilege for a Pages deploy: read the repo, write Pages, mint the OIDC
# token deploy-pages exchanges.
permissions:
  contents: read
  pages: write
  id-token: write

# Never run two Pages deploys at once; let an in-flight deploy finish.
concurrency:
  group: pages
  cancel-in-progress: false

jobs:
  build:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v5

      - name: Assemble the Pages site from PRIVACY.md
        run: |
          set -euo pipefail
          mkdir -p site
          # The policy page: a permalink pins the public path; the body is
          # PRIVACY.md verbatim (single source of truth — no duplicated copy).

1	# CrosswordChat — Architecture
2	
3	One rule drives the layout: **each hard problem lives in its own folder, testable without the
4	others.** The NYT DOM, the crossword semantics, the dialog policy, the phonetics, and the speech
5	plumbing are five different problems; none imports another's internals.
6	
7	## 1. Runtime topology (who runs where)
8	
9	```
10	┌─────────────────────────── Chrome ───────────────────────────────┐
11	│                                                                  │
12	│  Service worker (background/)  "switchboard + mouth"             │
13	│  · icon click → start/stop the in-page session                   │
14	│  · one-session bookkeeping, badge                                │
15	│  · per-tab icon variant + unsupported popup (URL-gated)          │
16	│  · chrome.tts relay (speak/cancel) — content scripts can't       │
17	│         ▲                                                        │
18	│         │ port (session registration + speak/done/cancel)        │
19	│         ▼                                                        │
20	│  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────┐                │
21	│  │ NYT crossword tab — content script           │                │
22	│  │  "brain + ears + hands", speech-only UI      │                │
23	│  │  · toolbar toggle button (start/stop in-page)│                │
24	│  │  · orchestrator (app/) · conversation machine│                │
25	│  │  · matching · STT port (mic, page origin)    │                │
26	│  │  · page-adapter (read/write/watch)           │                │
27	│  │  · console diagnostics                       │                │
28	│  │  main-world script (probe)                   │                │
29	│  └──────────────────────────────────────────────┘                │
30	└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
31	```
32	
33	- **Why the brain is in the page (content script):** the product is deliberately speech-only — no
34	  panel or popup to host or babysit. Speech recognition needs a document; the page is one. The mic
35	  grant belongs to nytimes.com (prompted once, on first session), and the session's lifetime is the
36	  page's — reload/navigate ends it, which is the wanted behavior. See FEASIBILITY §2.
37	- **Why TTS stays in the service worker:** `chrome.tts` (immune to page autoplay rules) is not
38	  exposed to content scripts, so the session relays speak/cancel over its port.
39	
40	## 2. Module map (source of truth for "what goes where")
41	
42	```
43	extension/src/
44	  page-adapter/    NYT DOM in, NYT DOM out. The ONLY place 'xwd__' may appear (REQ-PAGE-011).
45	    selectors.js     every selector/class, one file, probe-checked
46	    reader.js        DOM → Snapshot (grid cells, clue runs, selection, solved signal);
47	                     isPaused — NYT's "Your puzzle is paused" veil (REQ-LIFE-017)
48	    writer.js        enterAnswer/clearEntry via click + synthetic keydown, verified re-read;
49	                     per-cell pencil mode via the toolbar toggle, user's state restored;
50	                     keepAlive — a keystroke sent on each heard command so NYT doesn't
51	                     auto-pause a quiet puzzle (REQ-LIFE-017)
52	    navigator.js     selectClue (click the clue list item)
53	    watcher.js       MutationObserver → {solved | selection | grid | paused} events
54	                     (session-scoped); paused ends the session (REQ-LIFE-017/011)
55	    splash.js        pre-puzzle "Ready to start solving?" veil: find + click Play (REQ-LIFE-016)
56	    session-button.js  the in-page start/stop toggle, injected right of NYT's pencil
57	                     (REQ-LIFE-012); waits for the toolbar, degrades to no-button
58	    probe.js         selector health report for the live page
59	    clue-html.js     clue innerHTML → [{text, italic}] runs (pure; entities decoded)
60	  puzzle-model/    Crossword semantics. Pure.
61	    model.js         numbering, clue↔cells, crossings, patterns, progress, full-vs-solved
62	  matching/        Phonetics ↔ orthography. Pure.
63	    normalize.js     tokenize, digits/ordinals→words, A–Z normalization
64	    homophone-data.js  bundled dictionary (word sets + letter names + NATO)
65	    evaluate.js      utterance alternatives × entry → fit | ambiguous | collision | length-mismatch
66	    commands.js      command lexicon → intents (next/hint/answer …)
67	  conversation/    Dialog policy. Pure.
68	    machine.js       (state, event) → {state', actions[]}  — the "what to do next" algorithm
69	    strategies.js    next-clue selection: list-order, most-filled
70	    phrases.js       every English string; clue verbalizer (italics/brackets/?/blank/length)
71	  speech/          Browser speech plumbing. Injectable for tests.
72	    tts-port.js      chrome.tts | speechSynthesis → speak()/cancel() (used by the service worker)
73	    remote-tts-port.js  same contract from the content script: relays speak/cancel over the port
74	    stt-port.js      webkitSpeechRecognition → listenOnce() n-best, error taxonomy, mic preflight
75	  settings/        Persisted user settings (REQ-NAV-012). With options/, the ONLY place
76	    settings.js      allowed to touch chrome.storage (REQ-NFR-002): load/save/sanitize
77	  options/         The settings popup (right-click the toolbar icon → Settings…), anchored
78	                   under the icon via chrome.action.openPopup — no chrome://extensions detour
79	    options.html     reading-speed slider + strategy picker + Reset/Save buttons (copied to
80	                     dist/ by the build)
81	    options.js       wires the form to settings.js; edits are buffered, Save persists and
82	                     closes, Reset puts the defaults back in the form
83	  app/
84	    orchestrator.js  executes machine actions via ports/pageClient; owns the event loop
85	  background/
86	    service-worker.js  icon toggle, single-session bookkeeping, badge, chrome.tts relay,
87	                       per-tab icon variant + unsupported-site popup (REQ-LIFE-013/014),
88	                       Settings… context-menu item → settings popup under the icon
89	  popup/
90	    unsupported.html   static popup for unsupported tabs (REQ-LIFE-014); set per tab via
91	                       chrome.action.setPopup — supported tabs have no popup at all
92	  content/
93	    content-script.js  hosts the session: orchestrator + STT + page-adapter, console diagnostics;
94	                       inert until asked (REQ-NFR-004) apart from mounting the toolbar button
95	                       (REQ-LIFE-012), which starts/stops sessions from inside the page
96	    main-world.js      optional in-page probe helper (window.gameData presence)
97	  shared/
98	    messages.js      message type constants shared by content/background
99	    urls.js          supported-puzzle URL matcher (REQ-LIFE-013) — icon + popup gating
100	```
101	
102	**Dependency direction (enforced by review + arch test):**
103	`page-adapter` and `speech` touch browsers; `puzzle-model`, `matching`, `conversation` are pure and
104	import nothing from the impure layers. `app/orchestrator` is the only place all of them meet.
105	
106	## 3. Data contracts
107	
108	### Snapshot (page-adapter → everyone; the only puzzle input)
109	```js
110	{
111	  status: 'active' | 'solved' | 'not-found',
112	  size: { rows, cols },
113	  cells: [{ index, row, col, block, letter /* '' if empty */, penciled /* NYT pencil mode */,
114	            number /* or null */ }],
115	  clues: [{ id: 'A1', number: 1, direction: 'across', runs: [{ text, italic }] }],
116	  selection: { clueId: 'A1' | null, cellIndex: number | null }
117	}
118	```
119	Cell indices are row-major DOM order. Clue `runs` preserve formatting for the verbalizer.
120	`cellIndices` per clue are *derived* in the model (numbering algorithm), then cross-checked against
121	DOM numbers (REQ-MODEL-001) — the page adapter stays dumb.
122	
123	### Machine events (into `machine.reduce`)
124	`START{snapshot,settings}` · `TTS_DONE` · `HEARD{alternatives:[{transcript,confidence}]}` · `BARGE_IN` ·
125	`STT_ERROR{code}` · `ENTRY_RESULT{ok,snapshot}` · `UNDO_RESULT{ok,snapshot}` ·
126	`PAGE_EVENT{kind,snapshot}` · `TOGGLE_OFF`
127	
128	### Machine actions (out of `machine.reduce`)
129	`SAY{say:{kind,...}}` · `LISTEN` · `ENTER{clueId,word,cells}` · `UNDO{clueId,cells}` ·
130	`SELECT_CLUE{clueId}` · `END`
131	
132	`cells` entries are `{index, letter, pencil?}` — an optional `pencil: true` writes the letter in
133	NYT pencil mode, `pencil: false` explicitly rewrites it in pen (REQ-ANS-019: an override's ENTER
134	carries the malformed crossings' surviving letters as pencil rewrites; the matching UNDO carries
135	them back as pen rewrites).
136	
137	The machine is a **pure reducer**: same state + event → same actions, every time. That makes the
138	entire dialog policy (the trickiest behavior in the product) unit-testable as data — every
139	lifecycle requirement in REQUIREMENTS §5–§11 is asserted against action traces, no browser needed.
140	`SAY` payloads are *semantic* (`{kind:'collision', collisions:[...]}`); `phrases.js` turns them
141	into English at the edge. Policy tests don't break when wording changes; wording tests live with
142	the verbalizer.
143	
144	## 4. The main loop (orchestrator)
145	
146	```
147	dispatch(event):
148	  {state, actions} = machine.reduce(state, event)
149	  for a of actions:
150	    SAY         → console line + tts.speak(phrases.render(a.say)) → dispatch(TTS_DONE)
151	                  (a barge-in mic runs alongside the speech — REQ-SPCH-009: echo-guarded
152	                   input cancels the utterance and dispatches HEARD when the utterance
153	                   ends in listening; otherwise only stop is honored → BARGE_IN)
154	    LISTEN      → stt.listenOnce() → dispatch(HEARD | STT_ERROR)
155	    ENTER       → pause watcher → pageClient.enterAnswer(...) → dispatch(ENTRY_RESULT)
156	    UNDO        → pause watcher → clearEntry(blank-before cells) + enterAnswer(overwritten
157	                   letters) → dispatch(UNDO_RESULT) — reverts the last entry (REQ-ANS-017)
158	    SELECT_CLUE → pageClient.selectClue(...)
159	    END         → teardown (cancel tts/stt, stop watcher, disconnect port)
160	```
161	Strictly sequential; no queues, no races. Watcher events are suppressed while we write (our own
162	typing must not look like user activity — REQ-NAV-008's echo-loop clause).
163	
164	## 5. Message protocol (content ⇄ background)
165	
166	Page operations need no messages anymore — the orchestrator calls the page adapter directly
167	(same document). What's left is session control and the TTS relay:
168	
169	- Background → content (via `chrome.tabs.sendMessage`): `{type:'cc:start'}` — begin a session.
170	  Debug-only, from the service-worker console: `{type:'cc:ping'}` · `{type:'cc:snapshot'}` →
171	  Snapshot · `{type:'cc:probe'}` → report (MT-01).
172	- Content ⇄ background (long-lived Port `cc-session`): connect = session registered (badge ON;
173	  a pre-existing session on another tab is closed here — REQ-LIFE-009);
174	  `{type:'cc:speak', id, text}` → `chrome.tts` → `{type:'cc:speak-done', id}` ·
175	  `{type:'cc:tts-cancel'}` — immediate silence · `{type:'cc:close'}` (background → content: icon
176	  toggle / takeover) · disconnect = session over (badge cleared, in-flight speech cancelled).
177	- The in-page toggle button (REQ-LIFE-012) needs no messages of its own: it starts/stops the
178	  session directly in the content script, and the service worker finds out the way it always
179	  does — the port connects or disconnects.
180	
181	## 6. Testing architecture (the executable-requirements machinery)
182	
183	| Layer | Harness | What it proves |
184	|---|---|---|
185	| `matching`, `puzzle-model`, `conversation` | vitest, pure node | REQ-ANS/MODEL/NAV/CMD/HINT/READ/LIFE policy — the bulk of the spec |
186	| `speech` ports | vitest + hand-rolled fake `SpeechRecognition`/`chrome.tts` | REQ-SPCH wrapper behavior, error taxonomy |
187	| `page-adapter` | vitest + jsdom against **`extension-test/fixtures/fake-nyt/`** — a faithful replica of the NYT crossword DOM (same classes, same keyboard behavior, congrats modal) | REQ-PAGE end to end without nytimes.com |
188	| Architecture rules | `extension-test/unit/arch.test.js` greps the tree | REQ-PAGE-011, REQ-NFR-001/002 |
189	| Live page, mic, audio | `dev/docs/MANUAL-TESTS.md` scripts MT-01… | everything a browser can't fake honestly |
190	| Traceability | `tools/trace.mjs` (`npm run trace`) | every Active REQ ↔ some test; no phantom IDs (REQ-NFR-006) |
191	
192	The fake page double-dips: it is the integration-test target **and** a local rehearsal stage —
193	`npm run fixture` serves it at `http://localhost:8787`, and `npm run build:dev` produces a build
194	whose content script also matches localhost, so the whole voice loop can be exercised without an
195	NYT subscription.
196	
197	## 7. Decisions log
198	
199	| # | Decision | Why | Revisit when |
200	|---|---|---|---|
201	| D1 | MV3 + the content script hosts the conversation, speech-only (rev. 2 — originally the side panel) | Speech recognition needs a document and the page is one; no UI wanted (captions dropped for console diagnostics); session dying with the page is desired | Offscreen document if page-lifetime coupling or the nytimes.com mic grant annoys |
202	| D2 | `chrome.tts` primary for output | Immune to page autoplay rules | speechSynthesis-only if voice quality disappoints |
203	| D3 | Synthetic click+keydown for writing | Matches user behavior; per-cell addressing beats cursor settings | MT-02 fails → fallbacks in FEASIBILITY §3 |
204	| D4 | Pure reducer for dialog policy | The spec is mostly dialog policy; reducers make it assertable | — |
205	| D5 | Semantic SAY payloads, English at the edge | Policy tests survive copy edits | i18n (REQ-NFR-005) |
206	| D6 | Plain ES modules + esbuild, no TS | Zero-config bundling for MV3; JSDoc where shapes matter | Team growth |
207	| D7 | Homophones via bundled dictionary + n-best STT | Client-side (REQ-NFR-001); alternatives catch what the dictionary misses | Dictionary gaps observed in MT-06 |
208	| D8 | Numbering derived, DOM cross-checked | Survives NYT markup drift; catches reader bugs | — |
209	| D9 | In-page toolbar button as the primary start control (rev. of "no visual UI") | The action icon is invisible while solving; a speech-bubble next to NYT's pencil makes the feature discoverable where it's used. One button, no other surface; injection quarantined in page-adapter | NYT toolbar redesign breaks the anchor (probe + graceful degradation cover it) |
210	| D10 | Per-tab action icon + unsupported-site popup, gated by URL prefix only | The icon should say where CrosswordChat works before anything loads; a popup explains "why not here" and gives a support contact — no "tabs" permission needed (URL-less tabs are simply unsupported) | Supported-URL list grows (shared/urls.js is the one place) |
211	| D11 | TTS-vs-listener conflict handled by the app-level echo guard, **not** by constraining the recognizer's capture | `webkitSpeechRecognition` owns its capture and exposes no hook for `MediaTrackConstraints`; Chrome's default AEC (playout loopback) already attenuates in-browser TTS but misses `chrome.tts`'s OS-rendered output, so the string-match echo guard (REQ-SPCH-005) stays necessary. `echoCancellation`/`noiseSuppression` are requested on the one capture we own (the mic preflight, REQ-SPCH-003) and the applied AEC state is logged for diagnosis. `suppressLocalAudioPlayback`/`restrictOwnAudio` are `getDisplayMedia` screen-capture constraints — inapplicable to a mic+TTS setup | The Web Speech API gains a stream/constraints hook, or TTS shifts to an in-browser playout path so Chrome's default AEC can reference and cancel it — `speechSynthesis` already renders through Chrome's mix (so it is already largely cancelled); `chrome.tts`'s OS-rendered output is the part the loopback misses. Note this is a *playout-path* choice, not a Web Audio one: neither `chrome.tts` nor `speechSynthesis` exposes a stream we could route through Web Audio, so Web Audio cannot carry TTS here (it stays confined to the ready ping) |

## 3. Data contracts

### Snapshot (page-adapter → everyone; the only puzzle input)
```js
{
  status: 'active' | 'solved' | 'not-found',
  size: { rows, cols },
  cells: [{ index, row, col, block, letter /* '' if empty */, penciled /* NYT pencil mode */,
            number /* or null */ }],
  clues: [{ id: 'A1', number: 1, direction: 'across', runs: [{ text, italic }] }],
  selection: { clueId: 'A1' | null, cellIndex: number | null }
}
```
Cell indices are row-major DOM order. Clue `runs` preserve formatting for the verbalizer.
`cellIndices` per clue are *derived* in the model (numbering algorithm), then cross-checked against
DOM numbers (REQ-MODEL-001) — the page adapter stays dumb.

### Machine events (into `machine.reduce`)
`START{snapshot,settings}` · `TTS_DONE` · `HEARD{alternatives:[{transcript,confidence}]}` · `BARGE_IN` ·
`STT_ERROR{code}` · `ENTRY_RESULT{ok,snapshot}` · `UNDO_RESULT{ok,snapshot}` ·
`PAGE_EVENT{kind,snapshot}` · `TOGGLE_OFF`

### Machine actions (out of `machine.reduce`)
`SAY{say:{kind,...}}` · `LISTEN` · `ENTER{clueId,word,cells}` · `UNDO{clueId,cells}` ·
`SELECT_CLUE{clueId}` · `END`

`cells` entries are `{index, letter, pencil?}` — an optional `pencil: true` writes the letter in
NYT pencil mode, `pencil: false` explicitly rewrites it in pen (REQ-ANS-019: an override's ENTER
carries the malformed crossings' surviving letters as pencil rewrites; the matching UNDO carries
them back as pen rewrites).

The machine is a **pure reducer**: same state + event → same actions, every time. That makes the
entire dialog policy (the trickiest behavior in the product) unit-testable as data — every
lifecycle requirement in REQUIREMENTS §5–§11 is asserted against action traces, no browser needed.
`SAY` payloads are *semantic* (`{kind:'collision', collisions:[...]}`); `phrases.js` turns them
into English at the edge. Policy tests don't break when wording changes; wording tests live with
the verbalizer.

## 4. The main loop (orchestrator)

```
dispatch(event):
  {state, actions} = machine.reduce(state, event)
  for a of actions:
    SAY         → console line + tts.speak(phrases.render(a.say)) → dispatch(TTS_DONE)
                  (a barge-in mic runs alongside the speech — REQ-SPCH-009: echo-guarded
                   input cancels the utterance and dispatches HEARD when the utterance
                   ends in listening; otherwise only stop is honored → BARGE_IN)
    LISTEN      → stt.listenOnce() → dispatch(HEARD | STT_ERROR)
    ENTER       → pause watcher → pageClient.enterAnswer(...) → dispatch(ENTRY_RESULT)
    UNDO        → pause watcher → clearEntry(blank-before cells) + enterAnswer(overwritten
                   letters) → dispatch(UNDO_RESULT) — reverts the last entry (REQ-ANS-017)
    SELECT_CLUE → pageClient.selectClue(...)
    END         → teardown (cancel tts/stt, stop watcher, disconnect port)
```
Strictly sequential; no queues, no races. Watcher events are suppressed while we write (our own
typing must not look like user activity — REQ-NAV-008's echo-loop clause).

## 5. Message protocol (content ⇄ background)

Page operations need no messages anymore — the orchestrator calls the page adapter directly
(same document). What's left is session control and the TTS relay:

- Background → content (via `chrome.tabs.sendMessage`): `{type:'cc:start'}` — begin a session.
  Debug-only, from the service-worker console: `{type:'cc:ping'}` · `{type:'cc:snapshot'}` →
  Snapshot · `{type:'cc:probe'}` → report (MT-01).
- Content ⇄ background (long-lived Port `cc-session`): connect = session registered (badge ON;
  a pre-existing session on another tab is closed here — REQ-LIFE-009);
  `{type:'cc:speak', id, text}` → `chrome.tts` → `{type:'cc:speak-done', id}` ·
  `{type:'cc:tts-cancel'}` — immediate silence · `{type:'cc:close'}` (background → content: icon
  toggle / takeover) · disconnect = session over (badge cleared, in-flight speech cancelled).
- The in-page toggle button (REQ-LIFE-012) needs no messages of its own: it starts/stops the
  session directly in the content script, and the service worker finds out the way it always
  does — the port connects or disconnects.

# browser-speech pack (local)

A pack for the **browser speech surfaces**: `SpeechRecognition` / `webkitSpeechRecognition`,
`chrome.tts`, `speechSynthesis`, and the microphone capture behind them. Declared by hand as
`local/browser-speech` in `.claudinite-settings.json`.

voice-driven web app — nothing in a rule's logic, rationale, or fix text is specific to this
repo, and the scan is repo-shape agnostic (see below), so the pack cannot pass vacuously green
somewhere laid out differently. This repo is where the rules were *discovered* and is the corpus
they are verified against; it is not what they are about.

**Why local, not a canon declaration:** the mounted canon shelf has no home for this facet. The
`chrome-extension` pack covers MV3 build/runtime gotchas and says nothing about speech;
`chrome-extension-release`, `node`, `github-actions`, `tidy-repo`, `spec-driven-product` and
`executable-requirements` are all orthogonal. Nothing here duplicates a canon rule.

**Provenance:** distilled from this repo's real usage — `extension/src/speech/` (`stt-port.js`,
`tts-port.js`, `remote-tts-port.js`, `biasing.js`), the sequential action loop in
`extension/src/app/orchestrator.js`, decisions D2 and D11 in `dev/docs/ARCHITECTURE.md`, the
`aec`/`od` diagnostics in `dev/docs/SESSION-LOG.md`, and the mic-teardown live check in issue
\#63. Nothing in it is invented.

**Promotion note:** the checks are written to be lifted as-is — repo-shape agnostic scan, API
contracts only, no project identifiers in any rule's logic or messages — so the central promote
stage should be able to move them into a canon `browser-speech` (or `web-speech`) technology pack
with only the `doc:` paths rewritten. The `RULES.md` prose is the part still worth re-reading for
project coupling at promote time: some of it records tuning this product measured (the pause
window) rather than a fact of the API. Until then it lives here.

# browser-speech pack (local)

A pack for the **browser speech surfaces**: `SpeechRecognition` / `webkitSpeechRecognition`,
`chrome.tts`, `speechSynthesis`, and the microphone capture behind them. Declared by hand as
`local/browser-speech` in `.claudinite-settings.json`.

**Every rule judges a browser API contract, not a product decision.** Each one holds in any
voice-driven web app — nothing in a rule's logic, rationale, or fix text is specific to this
repo, and the scan is repo-shape agnostic (see below), so the pack cannot pass vacuously green
somewhere laid out differently. This repo is where the rules were *discovered* and is the corpus
they are verified against; it is not what they are about.

**Why local, not a canon declaration:** the mounted canon shelf has no home for this facet. The
`chrome-extension` pack covers MV3 build/runtime gotchas and says nothing about speech;
`chrome-extension-release`, `node`, `github-actions`, `tidy-repo`, `spec-driven-product` and
`executable-requirements` are all orthogonal. Nothing here duplicates a canon rule.

**Provenance:** distilled from this repo's real usage — `extension/src/speech/` (`stt-port.js`,
`tts-port.js`, `remote-tts-port.js`, `biasing.js`), the sequential action loop in
`extension/src/app/orchestrator.js`, decisions D2 and D11 in `dev/docs/ARCHITECTURE.md`, the
`aec`/`od` diagnostics in `dev/docs/SESSION-LOG.md`, and the mic-teardown live check in issue
\#63. Nothing in it is invented.

**Promotion note:** the checks are written to be lifted as-is — repo-shape agnostic scan, API
contracts only, no project identifiers in any rule's logic or messages — so the central promote
stage should be able to move them into a canon `browser-speech` (or `web-speech`) technology pack
with only the `doc:` paths rewritten. The `RULES.md` prose is the part still worth re-reading for
project coupling at promote time: some of it records tuning this product measured (the pause
window) rather than a fact of the API. Until then it lives here.

- **Session-end context** — `z silence` after long `en` runs is normal; `z user` seconds
  after repeated failures is frustration; `z nyt-pause` means NYT idled us out.

.claudinite/shared/packs/claudinite-growth/skills/generate-project-instructions/SKILL.md

1	---
2	name: generate-project-instructions
3	description: Decompose a project into its pack facets (working-style class, technology, aspect, domain) and extract its working instructions into reusable canon packs plus the project's own local packs (.claudinite/local_packs/). Use when a project has no established working style yet, or it exhibits a facet no pack covers — during bootstrap of a fresh/empty repo, or on an uplevel request.
4	---
5	
6	# Generate project instructions — extract packs, not a project doc
7	
8	This skill grows the corpus's pack library using the project in front of you as the evidence, and
9	lands the project's own working rules where every project's do now: its **local packs**. The owner's
10	projects recur — not as wholes, but **along axes**: the same working style returns with a different
11	product, the same technology returns with a different working style, the same audience returns on a
12	different stack. The first project to exhibit a facet pays the cost of working out how that facet is
13	handled; a **canon** pack is how every later project sharing it starts from the answer instead of
14	re-deriving it — and what stays specific to *this* project lands in **its own local pack**, the same
15	pack machinery run from the project's tree.
16	
17	The deliverable is therefore **two kinds of pack**, never a single "how to work on this repo" document:
18	
19	- **Canon pack seeds and refinements** — one `packs/<facet>/` per facet where this project has real
20	  portable insight, each written as if this project didn't exist, proposed to Claudinite.
21	- **The project's own local pack(s)** — under `.claudinite/local_packs/<pack>/` in the project's tree:
22	  the project-specific working style, concrete values (real commands, paths, names, metrics), and the
23	  project-specific rules that *don't* generalize — carried the same way any pack carries them (a check
24	  in the pack's `rules`, an activity skill, prose in `RULES.md`, a scheduled task), not a thin doc.
25	  This is the project's normalized capture surface; its `CLAUDE.md` is a thin routing map to it, loaded
26	  through the pack system rather than `@import`.
27	
28	The failure mode this skill exists to prevent: investigating the repo and producing one competent "how
29	to work on this repo" document — real commands, real paths, this product's concepts — with the
30	reusable core never separated out and the project-specific core dumped as always-loaded prose. If
31	portable guidance ends up in a local pack (it should be a canon pack), or the project's file names end
32	up in a canon pack (they belong in the local pack), the split is wrong.
33	
34	## 1. Gather the evidence
35	
36	Read the project before writing a word: README and existing docs, `CLAUDE.md` and everything it
37	imports, dependency and build manifests, scripts and CI, the test layout, git history and recent
38	PRs/issues, and any conversation with the owner about how they want to work. You are collecting two
39	things, both grounded in what you actually find:
40	
41	- the **facets** this project exhibits (step 2), and
42	- every **candidate rule** — each convention, procedure, or quality bar the project works by — ready to
43	  be sorted by owner (step 3).
44	
45	Invent nothing. If a call that changes the outcome is genuinely open, ask the owner one focused
46	question (via the structured popup); otherwise take the sensible default and note it.
47	
48	## 2. Decompose into facets, and check the shelf per facet
49	
50	A project is a bundle of **facets**, each a candidate pack on its own axis:
51	
52	- **Class — the working style.** How work runs end to end: the loop by which a change is proposed,
53	  verified, and shipped; the production bar; audience and longevity. Test: the pack still fits a
54	  project on a different stack, for a different product idea.
55	- **Technology — the platform.** True for any project on that platform, whatever its class or product.
56	  Test: the pack still fits when the product and the working style change. The first project on a new
57	  platform mints its pack — an iPhone app arriving tomorrow mints `iphone-app` the same way
58	  `chrome-extension` and `aws-sam` were minted.
59	- **Aspect — a separable slice of concern**, usually with its own on-switch. `chrome-extension-release`
60	  is the same technology as `chrome-extension` at a different moment: the release/store standard a
61	  project declares only once it ships. Split an aspect out of its parent facet when its rules activate
62	  at a different time or under a different decision than the parent's.
63	- **Domain — the audience or setting**, when it changes how work is done. A children's-app pack would
64	  carry design-review, requirement-processing, and compliance rules that hold whether the app is
65	  Flutter or web; a regulated-industry pack likewise. A domain that doesn't change the working rules
66	  isn't a facet worth a pack.
67	
68	**The product itself is never a facet** — "this specific product" doesn't recur, by definition; its
69	rules land in the project's own local pack.
70	
71	And a *statement of what the product does* isn't a pack rule at all — not even a local one. A pack, canon
72	or local, homes **how we work**: the conventions, gotchas and review discipline that recur across tasks
73	whatever the feature happens to be. The working-discipline rules bar the requirement-shaped rule outright;
74	here, catch it wearing a convention's clothes — a rule asserting which entities exist, what a surface must
75	render, or that a feature's parts are wired to each other. Pack-worthiness
76	is a question about the *work*, not about how load-bearing the code is — a real gap in product coverage is a
77	requirements gap, and answering it with a pack is how a feature's spec ends up somewhere nothing executes it.
78	
79	<example>
80	One extension project can exhibit four facets at once: `spec-driven-product` (class),
81	`chrome-extension` + `node` (technologies), `chrome-extension-release` (aspect, once it ships) — and
82	its local pack holds only what none of them own.
83	</example>
84	
85	Then check the canon shelf **per facet** (`packs/` here; the mounted `.claudinite/packs/` in a
86	consuming repo — a facet already owned by a *canon* pack is declared, not re-authored locally):
87	
88	- **Covered** → declare it (technology facets are usually already declared from the fingerprint) and
89	  move on — unless this project's evidence **sharpens or contradicts** the pack, which becomes a
90	  refinement PR to that pack, not a fork. Each further project of a facet is another exemplar: the
91	  pack should read as the intersection-plus-union of all of them, and a rule only one exemplar
92	  supports should say so or wait.
93	- **Uncovered, with real portable insight in the evidence** → this skill mints it (steps 3–4).
94	- **Uncovered, but this project has nothing durable to say about it yet** → leave it; a pack of
95	  placeholders helps nobody.
96	
97	Write each facet down — a short name plus one defining sentence — before drafting anything; every
98	sorting decision in step 3 tests against them.
99	
100	## 3. Sort every candidate rule to the single facet that owns it
101	
102	For each rule from step 1, apply the **portability strip per facet**: delete from the rule everything
103	the facet doesn't keep, and see whether something meaningful survives.
104	
105	- Delete the product and the stack, keep the loop — survives? → the **class** pack (canon).
106	- Delete the product and the working style, keep the platform — survives? → the **technology** (or
107	  **aspect**) pack (canon).
108	- Delete the stack, keep the audience/setting — survives? → the **domain** pack (canon).
109	- Survives nothing → project-specific: the project's **own local pack**.
110	
111	Route each rule to **exactly one owner** — the facet whose whole population the rule serves. "True for
112	any Node service" belongs to the canon `node` pack, not to this project's class pack, even if every
113	project of the class happens to use Node. Rewrite what lands in a canon pack project-agnostically and
114	parameterized, the way research-project does ("read *input* as whatever it means for your project").
115	
116	Then gate **every** pack-bound rule — canon or local — on the promotion ladder
117	([engine/checks/DESIGN.md](../../../../engine/checks/DESIGN.md)): a rule a deterministic **check** could enforce, or a
118	procedure with a nameable trigger a **skill** could carry, becomes that (in a canon seed it's flagged

# Generate project instructions — extract packs, not a project doc

This skill grows the corpus's pack library using the project in front of you as the evidence, and
lands the project's own working rules where every project's do now: its **local packs**. The owner's
projects recur — not as wholes, but **along axes**: the same working style returns with a different
product, the same technology returns with a different working style, the same audience returns on a
different stack. The first project to exhibit a facet pays the cost of working out how that facet is
handled; a **canon** pack is how every later project sharing it starts from the answer instead of
re-deriving it — and what stays specific to *this* project lands in **its own local pack**, the same
pack machinery run from the project's tree.

The deliverable is therefore **two kinds of pack**, never a single "how to work on this repo" document:

- **Canon pack seeds and refinements** — one `packs/<facet>/` per facet where this project has real
  portable insight, each written as if this project didn't exist, proposed to Claudinite.
- **The project's own local pack(s)** — under `.claudinite/local_packs/<pack>/` in the project's tree:
  the project-specific working style, concrete values (real commands, paths, names, metrics), and the
  project-specific rules that *don't* generalize — carried the same way any pack carries them (a check
  in the pack's `rules`, an activity skill, prose in `RULES.md`, a scheduled task), not a thin doc.
  This is the project's normalized capture surface; its `CLAUDE.md` is a thin routing map to it, loaded
  through the pack system rather than `@import`.

The failure mode this skill exists to prevent: investigating the repo and producing one competent "how
to work on this repo" document — real commands, real paths, this product's concepts — with the
reusable core never separated out and the project-specific core dumped as always-loaded prose. If
portable guidance ends up in a local pack (it should be a canon pack), or the project's file names end
up in a canon pack (they belong in the local pack), the split is wrong.

## 1. Gather the evidence

Read the project before writing a word: README and existing docs, `CLAUDE.md` and everything it
imports, dependency and build manifests, scripts and CI, the test layout, git history and recent
PRs/issues, and any conversation with the owner about how they want to work. You are collecting two
things, both grounded in what you actually find:

- the **facets** this project exhibits (step 2), and
- every **candidate rule** — each convention, procedure, or quality bar the project works by — ready to
  be sorted by owner (step 3).

Invent nothing. If a call that changes the outcome is genuinely open, ask the owner one focused
question (via the structured popup); otherwise take the sensible default and note it.

## 2. Decompose into facets, and check the shelf per facet

A project is a bundle of **facets**, each a candidate pack on its own axis:

- **Class — the working style.** How work runs end to end: the loop by which a change is proposed,
  verified, and shipped; the production bar; audience and longevity. Test: the pack still fits a
  project on a different stack, for a different product idea.
- **Technology — the platform.** True for any project on that platform, whatever its class or product.
  Test: the pack still fits when the product and the working style change. The first project on a new
  platform mints its pack — an iPhone app arriving tomorrow mints `iphone-app` the same way
  `chrome-extension` and `aws-sam` were minted.
- **Aspect — a separable slice of concern**, usually with its own on-switch. `chrome-extension-release`
  is the same technology as `chrome-extension` at a different moment: the release/store standard a
  project declares only once it ships. Split an aspect out of its parent facet when its rules activate
  at a different time or under a different decision than the parent's.
- **Domain — the audience or setting**, when it changes how work is done. A children's-app pack would
  carry design-review, requirement-processing, and compliance rules that hold whether the app is
  Flutter or web; a regulated-industry pack likewise. A domain that doesn't change the working rules
  isn't a facet worth a pack.

**The product itself is never a facet** — "this specific product" doesn't recur, by definition; its
rules land in the project's own local pack.

And a *statement of what the product does* isn't a pack rule at all — not even a local one. A pack, canon
or local, homes **how we work**: the conventions, gotchas and review discipline that recur across tasks
whatever the feature happens to be. The working-discipline rules bar the requirement-shaped rule outright;
here, catch it wearing a convention's clothes — a rule asserting which entities exist, what a surface must
render, or that a feature's parts are wired to each other. Pack-worthiness
is a question about the *work*, not about how load-bearing the code is — a real gap in product coverage is a
requirements gap, and answering it with a pack is how a feature's spec ends up somewhere nothing executes it.

12	// that is worth stating next to the capture-derived counts they land beside.
13	
14	// The five things a slot scheduler run could do with a due task. One name per
15	// outcome, used verbatim as the counter key in the aggregate, so there is no
16	// mapping table between "what the run said" and "what the fold counted" to drift.
17	export const TASK_RUN_OUTCOMES = Object.freeze([
18	  // A dispatch issue was filed: an agent session ran this task.
19	  'agent',
20	  // The task ran with NO agent — an `agent_model: none` task (code-work is the
21	  // whole task), or an agentful one whose code-work requested no agent phase.
22	  // Kebab, not the declaration field's `code_work`: this word is a WIRE token,
23	  // constrained to the line format's `[a-z-]+` charset.
24	  'code-work',
25	  // Due, but its precondition said there was nothing to do.
26	  'skipped',
27	  // Its code-work failed; the run converged the task to a needs-human issue.
28	  'failed',
29	  // Due and past its precondition, but no NEW agent run started: this slot was
30	  // already dispatched (exactly-once), an earlier dispatch is still open
31	  // (at-most-one-open), or another task claimed the run exclusively. Work that
32	  // was wanted and did not happen this run.
33	  'deferred',
34	]);
35	
36	// An empty per-task counter row — every outcome present, zeros included, so a row's
37	// shape never depends on which outcomes a task happened to hit.
38	export const emptyTaskRun = () => Object.fromEntries(TASK_RUN_OUTCOMES.map((o) => [o, 0]));
39	
40	// The line format. `v1` is the shape's version: a reader that meets a `v2` line
41	// knows it is looking at something it was not written for, instead of silently
42	// half-parsing it.
43	export const TASK_RUN_TAG = 'claudinite-task-run';
44	const VERSION = 'v1';
45	
46	// Actions stamps every log line with its own timestamp before the command's output,
47	// so the parse tolerates that prefix — without it, a fetched log reads as having
48	// printed nothing at all.
49	const LINE_RE = new RegExp(
50	  String.raw`^(?:\S+\s+)?${TASK_RUN_TAG} ${VERSION} (\S+)/(\S+) \[(\S+)\] ([a-z-]+)\s*$`,
51	);
52	
53	// One line → `{ pack, task, slotId, outcome }`, or null for anything that is not a
54	// record of this version. Deliberately strict: an unknown outcome word is NOT a
55	// record, because counting it would mint a counter key nothing ever reads.
56	// The code phase has been renamed twice, and job logs outlive both renames:
57	// `preprocess` (pre-2026-08-06) and `prework` (pre-2026-08-18) are the earlier
58	// words for what is now `code-work`. Runs logged under either still parse, each
59	// normalized straight to the canonical word.
60	// Exported because the outcome words are also the usage aggregate's counter KEYS,
61	// and that file holds rows written under the older words. Its decode renames them
62	// by this same map, so a rename never silently drops a historical count.
63	export const LEGACY_TASK_RUN_OUTCOMES = Object.freeze({ preprocess: 'code-work', prework: 'code-work' });
64	
65	export function parseTaskRun(line) {
66	  const m = LINE_RE.exec(line);
67	  if (!m) return null;
68	  const [, pack, task, slotId, word] = m;
69	  const outcome = LEGACY_TASK_RUN_OUTCOMES[word] ?? word;
70	  if (!TASK_RUN_OUTCOMES.includes(outcome)) return null;
71	  return { pack, task, slotId, outcome };
72	}
73	
74	// Every record in one job log. The log is the whole job's output — this picks its
75	// own lines out of it and ignores everything else.
76	export function parseTaskRuns(text) {
77	  const out = [];
78	  for (const line of String(text ?? '').split('\n')) {
79	    const rec = parseTaskRun(line);
80	    if (rec) out.push(rec);
81	  }
82	  return out;
83	}
84	
85	// --- executor-side execution records ------------------------------------------
86	// The historical records above say what the retired slot scheduler DID with a due
87	// task; these record what an EXECUTOR SESSION did with the work it ran. Printed by executor-side code
88	// (resolve-dispatch on a terminal verdict, record-exec.mjs at convergence), they
89	// land in the session transcript, ride to the conversation-logs branch with the
90	// executor's capture step, and the usage fold counts them deterministically —
91	// the "task statuses out of the conversation logs" half of the census (owner,
92	// 2026-08-06). Same single-home rule: renderer and parser sit here together.
93	
94	export const TASK_EXEC_STATUSES = Object.freeze([
95	  // The dispatch ran to completion within its ceiling; the issue was closed.
96	  'success',
97	  // The run failed (task failure or ceiling violation); converged to needs-human.
98	  'failed',
99	  // The dispatch named a task the repo no longer carries (file gone, pack
100	  // undeclared) — the executor closed the issue as obsolete. Not a failure.
101	  'task-gone',
102	  // The dispatch was malformed (bad path shape, unparseable declaration) and was
103	  // converged to needs-human without running.
104	  'invalid',
105	]);
106	
107	export const TASK_EXEC_TAG = 'claudinite-task-exec';
108	
109	// The bracketed field is the OCCURRENCE'S IDENTITY, which is a different thing under
110	// each dispatch mechanism: a slot id (`d2026-08-06`) where slots decide what runs, and
111	// the work item's issue number (`#867`) where the queue does. `slotId` keeps its name
112	// for the fielded records that already carry one; what it must never become is a
113	// constant, since it is the only join from a record back to the work it describes.
114	export const renderTaskExec = ({ pack, task, slotId, status }) =>
115	  `${TASK_EXEC_TAG} ${VERSION} ${pack}/${task} [${slotId ?? 'unknown'}] ${status}`;
116	
117	const EXEC_LINE_RE = new RegExp(
118	  String.raw`(?:^|\s)${TASK_EXEC_TAG} ${VERSION} (\S+)/(\S+) \[(\S+)\] ([a-z-]+)\s*$`,
119	);
120	
121	export function parseTaskExec(line) {
122	  const m = EXEC_LINE_RE.exec(line);
123	  if (!m) return null;
124	  const [, pack, task, slotId, status] = m;
125	  if (!TASK_EXEC_STATUSES.includes(status)) return null;
126	  return { pack, task, slotId, status };
127	}
128	
129	export function parseTaskExecs(text) {
130	  const out = [];
131	  for (const line of String(text ?? '').split('\n')) {
132	    const rec = parseTaskExec(line);
133	    if (rec) out.push(rec);
134	  }
135	  return out;
136	}
